chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hammad ibn Isa from Sawwar from Al-Hasan said:

Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him), when he defeated Talhah and Al-Zubayr, the people came retreating. They passed by a pregnant woman on the side of the road, and she was frightened by them, so she cast out what was in her womb. It struggled until it died, then its mother died after it. Ali (peace be upon him) and his companions passed by her while she was lying there and her child on the road. He asked them about her matter, and they said, 'She was pregnant; she was frightened when she saw the fighting and the retreat.' He asked them, 'Which one died before the other?' It was said, 'Her son died before her.' So he summoned her husband, Abu Al-Ghulam, the deceased, and bequeathed to him from the blood money of his son two-thirds of the diyyah. And he bequeathed to her mother one-third of the diyyah. Then he bequeathed to the husband from the deceased wife one-half of the one-third of the diyyah that she had inherited from her son, and he bequeathed to the relatives of the deceased wife the remainder. Then he bequeathed to the husband also from the blood money of his deceased wife one-half of the diyyah, which is two thousand and five hundred dirhams, and he bequeathed to the relatives of the deceased wife one-half of the diyyah, which is two thousand and five hundred dirhams. And that was because she had no other child besides the one she cast out when she was frightened. He said, 'And he paid all of that from the treasury of Basra.'
ai.seo_question: How is blood money distributed when a pregnant woman and her fetus die in the same incident?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates Imam Ali’s precise application of inheritance law during the Battle of the Camel, specifically addressing the complex scenario of a pregnant woman who died after expelling her fetus. It establishes the principle that the fetus, having been cast out and died, is treated as a distinct entity for diyyah distribution, thereby clarifying the shares of the husband, mother, and paternal relatives. This case is frequently cited by Shia jurists to demonstrate the practical implementation of *mawarith* (inheritance) rules in dynamic, real-world conflicts.
